raw_response:
I will keep my main base on the wheat-maize rotation, because that is the safest way for me to hold yield on a big farm like 163 mu. I have well water, so I can push fertilizer a bit and not leave the crop hungry. I do not start from zero every year. I start from what worked last year, then I adjust a little by crop price, labor, and water. Since some people in my house work off-farm, I will not put too much land into crops that need hand work every few days. That is why I will keep 100 mu in wheat-maize, and I will spread the other land across broccoli, chili, cotton, stevia, and watermelon. The wheat and maize are on the same 100 mu in rotation.

For wheat, I will feed it steadily and not save too hard on nitrogen, because if wheat is weak in spring, the loss is hard to recover. I will use improved seed, plough before wheat, give base fertilizer first, then topdress at jointing, and irrigate around sowing, jointing, and grain filling if water is needed. After wheat harvest, I will go straight into maize on the same land. For maize I will use hybrid seed, keep planting fast, and mostly do no-tillage to save time and hold moisture. I will put enough nitrogen on maize because this is one crop where being short costs grain fast.

For the cash crops, I will keep them on manageable areas and feed them more carefully. Broccoli, chili, and watermelon all need stronger fertilizer and more water, but they also give me better return if the market is decent. Cotton is slower but steadier, so I will keep a fair block there. Stevia I will keep smaller, just enough to spread risk. On all these crops I will watch what the stronger growers around me do, especially on spray timing, because missing one pest window can cost more than one extra spray. I would rather spend a bit more on fertilizer and one more pass of pesticide than lose the stand or lose the fruit set.
